newsitem.title: USA: Carter-Wallace up on bid, but market wary.
newsitem.headline: Carter-Wallace up on bid, but market wary.

text.p: Shares of Carter-Wallace Inc rose sharply after billionaire investor Marvin Davis disclosed an $835 million acquisition offer, but traders said the closely-held drug and consumer products company is not likely to be forced into a transaction with the financier.
Shares of Carter-Wallace rose 3-3/4 to 15-1/2, well below Davis' offer of $18 per share.
"I think the board is going to be completely unreceptive to this," said one trader of takeover stocks.
Carter-Wallace has long been rumored as an acquisition candidate.
Based on the company's 46.4 million outstanding shares, the market valued the acquisition offer at $835 million.
Wall Street sources said Carter-Wallace insiders control about 82 percent of the company via common stock and a special class of shares.
"With all of that control, they can do a 'just say no defense'," said another arbitrageur.
The company earlier confirmed it received a letter from Davis proposing the acquisition of all outstanding shares.
Carter-Wallace said it has referred the letter to its majority shareholder, the CPI Development Corp.

Market sources speculated that Davis has been buying up shares of the company in recent weeks. A spokeswoman for Davis said he had a "material interest" in Carter-Wallace, but she declined to be specific.

Carter-Wallace is known for consumer brands such as Trojan condoms, Arrid deoderant and Nair depilatory. It has been criticized by shareholders for a low stock price, but the company earlier this year said it had no plans to sell.
A shareholder proposal earlier this year to consider a merger was defeated.

Carter-Wallace ran into trouble in 1994 when the Food and Drug Administration advised physicians to stop prescribing its Felbatol epilepsy drug due to links with a blood disease. The company's stock also was hurt by other regulatory concerns about its pharmaceutical products.

Just last month Carter-Wallace named Ralph Levine to the posts of president and chief operating officer. Previously vice president, secretary and general counsel, Levine was named to succeed a retiring executive.

The 70-year-old Davis is well known on Wall Street for his corporate investments. A former chairman of Paramount, he was one of several dissident shareholders of MESA Inc who tried to wrest control of MESA from oilman Boone Pickens. Pickens eventually passed control of the company to financier Richard Rainwater.
The Davis spokeswoman said Davis is no longer involved in MESA.
Davis is currently developing a riverboat casino and entertainment center in Boonville, Mo.
